reviewNote: Original exercises with independently checked verification keys. AI-reviewed, not faculty-certified. Eight starter families do not exhaust the assigned syllabus.

problems.subject: Classical Mechanics
problems.title: Energy on a frictionless incline
problems.prompt: A 2.00 kg block starts from rest and slides down a frictionless track through a vertical drop of 1.25 m. Find its speed at the bottom. Explain why the mass does or does not matter.
problems.focus: Use uniform g = 9.81 m/s^2 and neglect air resistance. Choose the bottom as zero gravitational potential and compare initial and final mechanical energy.
problems.referenceFamily: Energy on a frictionless incline

problems.subject: Classical Mechanics
problems.title: A pendulum's first pass through the bottom
problems.prompt: A 0.150 kg bob hangs from a taut, massless string of length 1.20 m. Release it from rest with the string 60.0 degrees from the downward vertical. Find its speed on its first pass through the bottom. Assume a fixed pivot, no air resistance or pivot friction, a pointlike bob, and uniform g = 9.81 m/s^2.
problems.focus: Express the vertical drop in terms of string length and angle, then conserve mechanical energy.
problems.referenceFamily: Energy on a frictionless incline

problems.subject: Classical Mechanics
problems.title: A skier reaches a lower ledge
problems.prompt: A skier moving at 4.00 m/s reaches a smooth downhill section that ends 2.00 m lower. Find the speed at the end. Treat the skier as a particle, neglect drag and friction, assume the track remains in contact with the skier and does no work, and use uniform g = 9.81 m/s^2.
problems.focus: Retain the initial kinetic energy when relating a height change to the final speed.
problems.referenceFamily: Energy on a frictionless incline

problems.subject: Classical Mechanics
problems.title: Two height markers on a vertical toss
problems.prompt: A small ball is thrown vertically upward at 12.0 m/s. Find the height above its launch point where its upward speed first becomes 5.00 m/s, and find its maximum height. Neglect air resistance and use uniform g = 9.81 m/s^2.
problems.focus: Solve the energy equation for an unknown elevation and identify the turning point.
problems.referenceFamily: Energy on a frictionless incline

problems.subject: Classical Mechanics
problems.title: A spring launches a cart uphill
problems.prompt: A cart of mass 0.500 kg rests against a horizontal ideal spring of constant 200 N/m, compressed by 0.200 m. On release the cart separates from the spring when the spring reaches its natural length and then climbs a smooth ramp. Find the greatest vertical height above the launch level. Neglect wheel rotation, friction, air resistance, and any spring mass; use g = 9.81 m/s^2.
problems.focus: Connect elastic potential energy at release to gravitational potential energy at the turning point.
problems.referenceFamily: Energy on a frictionless incline

problems.subject: Classical Mechanics
problems.title: A rough strip before a smooth ramp
problems.prompt: A 3.00 kg block enters a horizontal rough strip at 6.00 m/s. The strip is 2.00 m long and has kinetic-friction coefficient 0.200. After crossing it, the block climbs a frictionless ramp. Find the energy converted to thermal energy on the strip and the maximum height reached on the ramp, measured from the strip. Neglect drag, assume continuous contact, and use g = 9.81 m/s^2.
problems.focus: Subtract the work of kinetic friction before converting the remaining kinetic energy into height.
problems.referenceFamily: Energy on a frictionless incline

problems.subject: Classical Mechanics
problems.title: The lowest launch point for a loop
problems.prompt: A small block slides along the inside of a smooth vertical circular loop of radius R. It is released from rest on a smooth approach track at height H above the loop's bottom. Find the least H that lets it complete the loop while maintaining contact, and the speed at the bottom for that limiting release. Treat the block as a particle, neglect drag, assume the approach connects smoothly, and take uniform gravitational acceleration g.
problems.focus: Combine energy conservation with the nonnegative contact-force condition at the top of the loop.
problems.referenceFamily: Energy on a frictionless incline

problems.subject: Classical Mechanics
problems.title: A spring at the end of a rough landing
problems.prompt: A 1.00 kg block starts from rest 1.00 m above a horizontal landing and descends a frictionless ramp. On the landing it travels 1.00 m over a rough surface before contacting an initially uncompressed spring of constant 100 N/m. The same rough surface continues beneath the spring, with kinetic-friction coefficient 0.200 throughout. Find the block's speed just before spring contact and the maximum spring compression during its first forward motion. The spring is fixed, horizontal, ideal, and massless. Neglect drag and use g = 9.81 m/s^2.
problems.focus: Keep the additional friction work during compression and select the physical root of the resulting energy equation.
problems.referenceFamily: Energy on a frictionless incline

problems.subject: Classical Mechanics
problems.title: Small oscillations on a circular hoop
problems.prompt: A bead of mass m slides without friction on a fixed circular hoop of radius a in a vertical plane. Let theta be measured from the downward vertical. Use Lagrange's equation to derive the exact equation of motion and find the angular frequency of small oscillations about the bottom.
problems.focus: Use uniform downward gravitational acceleration g, neglect air resistance, and treat the bead as a particle. Construct kinetic and potential energies in the single allowed coordinate.
problems.referenceFamily: Small oscillations on a circular hoop

problems.subject: Classical Mechanics
problems.title: A hoop tilted toward horizontal
problems.prompt: A bead of mass m moves without friction on a stationary circular hoop of radius a. The hoop's plane makes an angle beta above the horizontal, with 0 < beta <= pi/2. Measure theta in that plane from the lowest point on the hoop. Derive a Lagrangian, the exact equation of motion, and the angular frequency of small oscillations around theta = 0. Gravity has constant magnitude g and points vertically downward; neglect drag.
problems.focus: Project gravitational height into the hoop's plane before applying the Euler-Lagrange equation.
problems.referenceFamily: Small oscillations on a circular hoop

problems.subject: Classical Mechanics
problems.title: Oscillations in an accelerating lift
problems.prompt: A vertical circular hoop of radius a is fixed inside a lift accelerating upward with constant acceleration A >= 0. A bead of mass m slides on it without friction. In coordinates attached to the lift, theta is measured from the downward vertical. Construct an effective Lagrangian in the lift frame, derive the exact equation for theta, and find the angular frequency of small oscillations at the bottom. Gravity is uniform with downward magnitude g; neglect drag.
problems.focus: Include the inertial force associated with the translating frame in the effective gravitational potential.
problems.referenceFamily: Small oscillations on a circular hoop

problems.subject: Classical Mechanics
problems.title: A descending capsule approaches free fall
problems.prompt: A vertical hoop of radius a is fixed in a capsule accelerating downward with a constant magnitude A, where 0 < A < g. A bead of mass m slides without friction. Use theta from the downward vertical in the capsule frame. Derive the exact angular equation and the small-oscillation period about the bottom. Find the ratio of that period to the period when the capsule is unaccelerated, and explain the limit A approaching g from below. Gravity has magnitude g; neglect drag.
problems.focus: Find the effective restoring force in a translating frame and interpret a vanishing frequency.
problems.referenceFamily: Small oscillations on a circular hoop

problems.subject: Classical Mechanics
problems.title: A charged bead in a sideways electric field
problems.prompt: A bead of mass m and positive charge q moves without friction on a fixed insulating circular hoop of radius a in a vertical plane. A uniform electric field of magnitude E >= 0 points horizontally to the right in that plane. Let theta be measured from the downward vertical, increasing toward the right. Gravity has downward magnitude g. Neglect drag, radiation, and polarization of the hoop. Derive the exact angular equation, locate the stable equilibrium connected to theta = 0 as E approaches zero, and find the small-oscillation angular frequency around it.
problems.focus: Combine two uniform forces into an effective gravity vector, or expand the potential at its displaced minimum.
problems.referenceFamily: Small oscillations on a circular hoop

problems.subject: Classical Mechanics
problems.title: A motor turns a vertical hoop slowly
problems.prompt: A motor rotates a vertical circular hoop of radius a about its vertical diameter at a prescribed constant angular speed Omega. A bead of mass m slides on the hoop without friction. Let theta be the angle from the downward vertical and assume 0 <= Omega^2 < g/a. In an inertial frame, derive the bead's kinetic energy and Lagrangian, then find the exact angular equation and the small-oscillation frequency about the bottom. Gravity is uniform with magnitude g; neglect drag.
problems.focus: Account for motion of the constraint in the kinetic energy and identify its effect on local stability.
problems.referenceFamily: Small oscillations on a circular hoop

problems.subject: Classical Mechanics
problems.title: How finite amplitude changes a hoop period
problems.prompt: A bead slides without friction on a stationary vertical circular hoop of radius a. Release it from rest at theta = theta_max, with 0 < theta_max < pi, where theta is measured from the downward vertical. Gravity has magnitude g. Derive an integral for the full oscillation period. Then obtain the first correction to the small-amplitude period through order theta_max^2, taking theta_max in radians, and state whether the period increases or decreases with amplitude. Neglect drag.
problems.focus: Use energy to obtain a period integral, then expand an integral with fixed endpoints.
problems.referenceFamily: Small oscillations on a circular hoop

problems.subject: Classical Mechanics
problems.title: New equilibria above the rotation threshold
problems.prompt: A frictionless bead of mass m moves on a vertical circular hoop of radius a whose vertical diameter is rotated by a motor at fixed angular speed Omega. Let theta run modulo 2pi from the downward vertical. Assume Omega^2 > g/a, uniform gravity g, and no drag. Starting from the kinetic energy of this moving constraint, find every equilibrium modulo 2pi, classify its stability, and derive the small-oscillation frequency at each stable equilibrium. Also give a conserved one-coordinate energy for theta and explain why the bead's inertial mechanical energy need not be conserved.
problems.focus: Analyze the curvature of the effective potential, distinguish it from ordinary mechanical energy, and check the near-threshold behavior.
problems.referenceFamily: Small oscillations on a circular hoop

problems.subject: Electricity & Magnetism
problems.title: Parallel-plate capacitor
problems.prompt: An air-filled parallel-plate capacitor has plate area 0.0200 m^2, separation 1.00 mm, and potential difference 12.0 V. Neglect fringing. Find its capacitance, the magnitude of charge on either plate, and the electric field between the plates.
problems.focus: Treat air as vacuum with epsilon_0 = 8.854 x 10^-12 F/m. Relate plate geometry, potential difference, and uniform electric field.
problems.referenceFamily: Parallel-plate capacitor

problems.subject: Electricity & Magnetism
problems.title: Reconstruct a capacitor gap
problems.prompt: A vacuum parallel-plate capacitor has plate area 0.0150 m^2 and measured capacitance 265.62 pF. When it is connected to a 9.00 V source, find the plate separation, the magnitude of charge on either plate, and the field magnitude in the gap. Neglect fringing and use epsilon_0 = 8.854 x 10^-12 F/m.
problems.focus: Infer geometry from capacitance, then relate the imposed potential difference to charge and field.
problems.referenceFamily: Parallel-plate capacitor

problems.subject: Electricity & Magnetism
problems.title: Pulling apart an isolated capacitor
problems.prompt: A vacuum parallel-plate capacitor initially has capacitance C_0 = 100 pF, separation d_0 = 1.00 mm, and voltage V_0 = 20.0 V. Disconnect the source so that charge cannot leak, and slowly increase the separation to 2d_0 without changing the plate area. Find the final capacitance, plate-charge magnitude, voltage, field magnitude, and the external work required. Neglect fringing, radiation, and dissipation; the plates begin and end at rest.
problems.focus: Hold charge fixed while changing geometry, and connect external work to the change in stored field energy.
problems.referenceFamily: Parallel-plate capacitor

problems.subject: Electricity & Magnetism
problems.title: Filling an isolated gap with dielectric
problems.prompt: A vacuum parallel-plate capacitor of capacitance C_0 = 200 pF and gap d = 2.00 mm is isolated with plate-charge magnitude Q = 6.00 nC. A homogeneous linear dielectric of relative permittivity 3.00 is inserted slowly until it fills the gap. Find the final capacitance, voltage, field magnitude, and the work done by the external agent during insertion. Assume no charge leakage, friction, or other dissipation, unchanged geometry, and negligible fringing. The dielectric starts and ends at rest.
problems.focus: Conserve free charge and use the total stored electrostatic energy of the linear dielectric capacitor.
problems.referenceFamily: Parallel-plate capacitor

problems.subject: Electricity & Magnetism
problems.title: A battery remains attached during dielectric insertion
problems.prompt: A vacuum parallel-plate capacitor has capacitance C_0 = 100 pF and remains connected to an ideal 10.0 V source while a linear dielectric of relative permittivity 4.00 slowly fills its gap. Find the final capacitance and plate-charge magnitude, the increase in stored energy, the work delivered by the source, and the work done by the external agent moving the dielectric. Neglect fringing, leakage, friction, and radiation; the dielectric begins and ends at rest. Define positive work as energy delivered to the capacitor-dielectric system.
problems.focus: Track source work as well as stored energy when voltage is held fixed.
problems.referenceFamily: Parallel-plate capacitor

problems.subject: Electricity & Magnetism
problems.title: Two materials stacked across a capacitor gap
problems.prompt: An isolated parallel-plate capacitor has plate area A, gap d, and free charges +Q and -Q, with Q > 0. A linear dielectric of relative permittivity 3 fills half the gap thickness over the full area; the other half is vacuum. The interface is parallel to the plates and carries no free charge. Find the electric-field magnitude in each half, the plate potential difference, and the equivalent capacitance. Neglect fringing and use vacuum permittivity epsilon_0.
problems.focus: Apply the normal-displacement boundary condition and add voltage drops across layers.
problems.referenceFamily: Parallel-plate capacitor

problems.subject: Electricity & Magnetism
problems.title: Sharing charge with an empty capacitor
problems.prompt: A capacitor of capacitance C initially has charges +CV_0 and -CV_0 on its plates, with V_0 > 0. A second capacitor of capacitance 2C is uncharged. With both disconnected from any source, connect corresponding plates in parallel through a resistor: the initially positive plate connects to one plate of the second capacitor, and the remaining plates connect together. After the current has stopped, find the common voltage, the charge magnitude on each capacitor, and the energy dissipated in the resistor. Treat the capacitors as ideal, ignore mutual capacitance and radiation, and assume the resistor is the only dissipative element.
problems.focus: Use charge conservation and a common final voltage, then account for the missing stored energy.
problems.referenceFamily: Parallel-plate capacitor

problems.subject: Electricity & Magnetism
problems.title: Separating plates while a source holds the voltage
problems.prompt: A vacuum parallel-plate capacitor has area A and is connected to an ideal source that holds the voltage at V > 0. An external agent slowly increases the separation from d to 2d. At an intermediate separation x, find the magnitude and direction of the electric force on either plate. Then find the external work, the work delivered by the source, and the change in stored energy over the full displacement. Neglect fringing, dissipation, and radiation; the plates start and end at rest. Use epsilon_0 and define positive work as energy delivered to the capacitor.
problems.focus: Use the force between plates and include charge exchanged with a constant-voltage source.
problems.referenceFamily: Parallel-plate capacitor

problems.subject: Electricity & Magnetism
problems.title: Field of a uniformly charged solid cylinder
problems.prompt: An infinitely long solid cylinder of radius a carries uniform volume charge density rho. Use Gauss's law to find the electric field at cylindrical radius s both inside and outside the cylinder. Check the result at s = a.
problems.focus: Treat the charge as a fixed insulating distribution in vacuum with permittivity epsilon_0. Use cylindrical symmetry; a signed rho fixes the field direction.
problems.referenceFamily: Field of a uniformly charged solid cylinder

problems.subject: Electricity & Magnetism
problems.title: An insulating cylindrical charge sheet
problems.prompt: An infinitely long, infinitesimally thin insulating cylindrical shell of radius a carries a uniform surface-charge density sigma > 0. The regions inside and outside are vacuum. Find the electric field for 0 <= s < a and s > a, where s is distance from the axis, and calculate the jump in its outward radial component across the shell. Use epsilon_0; assume electrostatic conditions and no other charges.
problems.focus: Compare enclosed charge in coaxial Gaussian cylinders and check the surface boundary condition.
problems.referenceFamily: Field of a uniformly charged solid cylinder

problems.subject: Electricity & Magnetism
problems.title: Choose a finite potential reference
problems.prompt: A fixed insulating cylinder of radius a is infinitely long and has uniform volume-charge density rho > 0 in vacuum. Find the electrostatic potential V(s) inside and outside it using V(a) = 0. State V(0), and explain whether a finite potential can instead be assigned by setting V at infinity to zero. Use cylindrical radius s and permittivity epsilon_0; no other charges are present.
problems.focus: Integrate the radial electric field with a finite reference and keep potential continuous at the boundary.
problems.referenceFamily: Field of a uniformly charged solid cylinder

problems.subject: Electricity & Magnetism
problems.title: Potential inside a charged cylindrical sheet
problems.prompt: An infinitely long insulating cylindrical sheet of radius a carries uniform surface-charge density sigma > 0 in vacuum. Find V(s) for 0 <= s < a and s > a with V(a) = 0. Also find the work done by the electric field when a test charge q > 0 moves quasistatically from radius 2a to radius 3a outside the shell. The test charge is too small to change the source distribution. Use epsilon_0 and neglect all other forces when calculating the field's work.
problems.focus: Integrate a radial field and distinguish work by the field from change in potential energy.
problems.referenceFamily: Field of a uniformly charged solid cylinder

problems.subject: Electricity & Magnetism
problems.title: A uniformly charged hollow cylinder
problems.prompt: An infinitely long insulating tube has inner radius a and outer radius b, with 0 < a < b. Its material carries uniform volume-charge density rho > 0 for a < s < b; the central cavity and the exterior are vacuum, and there are no surface-charge sheets. Find the electric field in all three radial regions and the potential difference V(0) - V(b). Use epsilon_0 and assume a fixed electrostatic charge distribution.
problems.focus: Track the enclosed charge through an empty cavity and integrate the field only where it is nonzero.
problems.referenceFamily: Field of a uniformly charged solid cylinder

problems.subject: Electricity & Magnetism
problems.title: A cylinder denser near its edge
problems.prompt: A fixed, infinitely long insulating cylinder of radius a has volume-charge density rho(s) = rho_0(s/a)^2 for 0 <= s <= a, where rho_0 > 0. Outside the cylinder the charge density is zero and space is vacuum. Find the electric field inside and outside, and the potential difference V(0) - V(a). Use epsilon_0, cylindrical radius s, and electrostatic conditions.
problems.focus: Integrate the radial density to get enclosed charge before applying Gauss's law.
problems.referenceFamily: Field of a uniformly charged solid cylinder

problems.subject: Electricity & Magnetism
problems.title: A displaced cylindrical cavity
problems.prompt: Start with an infinitely long insulating cylinder of radius b and uniform volume-charge density rho > 0. Remove an empty cylindrical cavity of radius a whose axis is parallel to the original axis but displaced by a transverse vector d_vec, with |d_vec| + a < b. The charge density in the remaining material stays fixed at rho, and everything is in vacuum. Show that the electric field is uniform throughout the cavity and find it. For two points P and Q in the cavity separated by the transverse vector ell_vec = r_Q - r_P, find V(Q) - V(P). Use epsilon_0; there are no conductors or other charges.
problems.focus: Use superposition of solid-cylinder fields when the cavity destroys symmetry about a single axis.
problems.referenceFamily: Field of a uniformly charged solid cylinder

problems.subject: Electricity & Magnetism
problems.title: The field energy of a coaxial capacitor
problems.prompt: An infinitely long solid conducting cylinder of radius a carries positive charge per unit length lambda. A coaxial conducting tube has inner radius b > a and outer radius c > b, and carries net charge per unit length -lambda. The gap and exterior are vacuum. In electrostatic equilibrium, find the electric field in each radial region away from the surfaces, the potential difference between the conductors, the capacitance per unit length, and the stored energy per unit length. Verify the energy using both the field-energy density and the capacitance. Use epsilon_0 and neglect end effects.
problems.focus: Combine conductor boundary conditions, Gauss's law, potential differences, and two equivalent energy descriptions.
problems.referenceFamily: Field of a uniformly charged solid cylinder

problems.subject: Quantum Mechanics
problems.problemFamily: Photon energy and the photoelectric effect
problems.title: Energy carried by a green photon
problems.prompt: A monochromatic green-light source emits photons of wavelength 500 nm in vacuum. Find the energy of one photon in eV and in joules. Use hc = 1240 eV nm and 1 eV = 1.602 × 10^−19 J. Treat the quoted constants and wavelength as exact for this exercise.
problems.focus: Relate photon energy to wavelength and convert an energy unit without confusing energy with power.
problems.referenceFamily: Photoelectric stopping potential

problems.subject: Quantum Mechanics
problems.problemFamily: Photon energy and the photoelectric effect
problems.title: Choose light above a cathode threshold
problems.prompt: A clean metal photocathode has work function 2.48 eV. Find its threshold wavelength and decide whether light of wavelength 620 nm can eject electrons. Use hc = 1240 eV nm. Assume the single-photon photoelectric model, initially bound electrons at the emission threshold, negligible thermal emission, and no applied field that lowers the work function. Define the threshold wavelength by photon energy equal to the work function.
problems.focus: Translate the emission threshold into a wavelength inequality.
problems.referenceFamily: Photoelectric stopping potential

problems.subject: Quantum Mechanics
problems.problemFamily: Photon energy and the photoelectric effect
problems.title: Photoelectric stopping potential
problems.prompt: Light of wavelength 400 nm illuminates a metal with work function 2.30 eV. Find the maximum photoelectron kinetic energy and the stopping potential. Use hc = 1240 eV nm.
problems.focus: Subtract the work function from photon energy and interpret the stopping potential as a positive magnitude.
problems.referenceFamily: Photoelectric stopping potential

problems.subject: Quantum Mechanics
problems.problemFamily: Photon energy and the photoelectric effect
problems.title: Stopping electrons from an ultraviolet source
problems.prompt: An ultraviolet lamp of wavelength 310 nm illuminates a metal with work function 2.70 eV. Find the maximum emitted-electron kinetic energy in eV and the stopping-potential magnitude in volts. Use hc = 1240 eV nm and the definition that an electron changes energy by 1 eV across a potential difference of magnitude 1 V. Assume single-photon emission and neglect contact potentials and thermal emission.
problems.focus: Apply the photoelectric energy balance and convert electron kinetic energy into a retarding voltage.
problems.referenceFamily: Photoelectric stopping potential

problems.subject: Quantum Mechanics
problems.problemFamily: Photon energy and the photoelectric effect
problems.title: Convert ultraviolet power into detector current
problems.prompt: A 400 nm beam delivers 2.00 μW of optical power to a photocathode with work function 2.30 eV. The external quantum efficiency is 5.00%, meaning that 0.0500 electron is emitted on average per incident photon at this wavelength. Find the photon arrival rate, the saturation photocurrent when all emitted electrons are collected, and the maximum photoelectron kinetic energy. Then predict how the current and maximum kinetic energy change if the optical power doubles at fixed wavelength. Use hc = 1240 eV nm, 1 eV = 1.602 × 10^−19 J, and electron-charge magnitude e = 1.602 × 10^−19 C. Assume independent single-photon emission, constant efficiency, and no space-charge loss or dark current.
problems.focus: Separate the number of photoelectrons per second from the energy available to each electron.
problems.referenceFamily: Photoelectric stopping potential

problems.subject: Quantum Mechanics
problems.problemFamily: Photon energy and the photoelectric effect
problems.title: Calibrate an unknown photocathode
problems.prompt: Two independent measurements of a photocathode give stopping-potential magnitudes of 2.50 V under 248 nm light and 1.50 V under 310 nm light. Determine the work function from each measurement and assess whether one work function explains both. Find the threshold wavelength and decide whether a 620 nm source should produce single-photon emission. Use hc = 1240 eV nm and e × 1 V = 1 eV. Treat the data as exact and neglect contact potentials, surface changes, and thermal emission.
problems.focus: Infer a material property from measured stopping voltages and test the model with a second observation.
problems.referenceFamily: Photoelectric stopping potential

problems.subject: Quantum Mechanics
problems.problemFamily: Photon energy and the photoelectric effect
problems.title: A retarding collector selects one of two colors
problems.prompt: Two beams illuminate a photocathode of work function 2.00 eV: a 248 nm beam supplies 1.00 μW and a 496 nm beam supplies 2.00 μW. The external quantum efficiency is 10.0% for each beam. In this idealized detector, every emitted electron from a given beam leaves normal to the surface with kinetic energy hc/λ minus the work function. A planar collector applies a retarding-potential magnitude U; an electron is collected only if its initial kinetic energy exceeds eU. Find the photocurrent at U = 0 and U = 1.00 V, and find the smallest U that blocks both electron populations under this rule. Use hc = 1240 eV nm, 1 eV = 1.602 × 10^−19 J, and e = 1.602 × 10^−19 C. Assume independent single-photon emission, constant efficiency, complete collection of electrons above the barrier, and no contact potentials or dark current.
problems.focus: Combine photon rates, photoelectric energy thresholds, and energy-selective collection in a fully specified ideal detector.
problems.referenceFamily: Photoelectric stopping potential

problems.subject: Quantum Mechanics
problems.problemFamily: Photon energy and the photoelectric effect
problems.title: Predict a detector response from calibration data
problems.prompt: A photocathode illuminated by 310 nm light at incident power 4.00 μW has stopping-potential magnitude 1.80 V and saturation photocurrent 80.0 nA. At 620 nm and the same incident power, it has no photocurrent. Infer the work function and the external quantum efficiency from the 310 nm measurements, and check whether the inferred work function explains the 620 nm observation. Then predict the stopping-potential magnitude and saturation current for 400 nm light at 2.00 μW. Use hc = 1240 eV nm, 1 eV = 1.602 × 10^−19 J, and e = 1.602 × 10^−19 C. Assume the external quantum efficiency is wavelength independent whenever the photon energy exceeds the work function, single-photon emission applies, all emitted electrons are collected at saturation, and contact potentials and dark current are negligible.
problems.focus: Infer separate energy and efficiency parameters, check a non-emitting case, and predict a new operating condition.
problems.referenceFamily: Photoelectric stopping potential

problems.subject: Quantum Mechanics
problems.title: Normalize the ground-state shape
problems.prompt: A particle is confined to an infinite square well with walls at x = 0 and x = L, where L > 0. Its spatial wavefunction is ψ(x) = A sin(πx/L) inside the well and zero outside. Choose A to be real and positive. Determine A from normalization, state its physical dimensions, and verify that the wavefunction satisfies both wall boundary conditions.
problems.focus: Normalize a continuous probability amplitude and distinguish amplitude dimensions from probability-density dimensions.
problems.referenceFamily: Probability in the middle third of a box

problems.subject: Quantum Mechanics
problems.title: Read the energy of a stationary box state
problems.prompt: A particle of mass m > 0 is in an infinite square well from x = 0 to x = L, with zero potential inside. Its normalized wavefunction is ψ(x) = √(2/L) sin(3πx/L) inside and zero outside. Apply the Hamiltonian H = −(ℏ²/2m)d²/dx² inside the well to determine the possible energy-measurement result and its probability. Express this energy as a multiple of the ground-state energy E₁ = π²ℏ²/(2mL²). Finally, compare it with the energy of the n = 3 state in a different well of width L/2 and the same mass. Here ℏ is the reduced Planck constant; the width comparison concerns two separately prepared stationary states.
problems.focus: Recognize an energy eigenstate and check how confinement energy scales with width.
problems.referenceFamily: Probability in the middle third of a box

problems.subject: Quantum Mechanics
problems.title: Probability in the middle third of a box
problems.prompt: A particle is in the ground state of an infinite square well from x = 0 to x = L. Find the probability of measuring it between x = L/3 and x = 2L/3.
problems.focus: Integrate the normalized ground-state probability density over the stated interval.
problems.referenceFamily: Probability in the middle third of a box

problems.subject: Quantum Mechanics
problems.title: A position detector near the left wall
problems.prompt: A particle in an infinite square well from x = 0 to x = L is prepared in ψ₂(x) = √(2/L) sin(2πx/L) inside the well and zero outside. An ideal position detector reports whether the particle lies in 0 < x < L/8. Find the probability that it reports yes, and compare it with the probability for a position uniformly distributed across the well. Assume a single position measurement on the stated normalized state; L > 0.
problems.focus: Calculate a spatial probability and use the boundary node to interpret its difference from a uniform distribution.
problems.referenceFamily: Probability in the middle third of a box

problems.subject: Quantum Mechanics
problems.title: A superposition moves probability between the two halves
problems.prompt: A particle of mass m in an infinite well from x = 0 to x = L has normalized stationary modes φₙ(x) = √(2/L) sin(nπx/L) and energies Eₙ = n²π²ℏ²/(2mL²). At t = 0 it is prepared in ψ(x,0) = [φ₁(x) + φ₂(x)]/√2 and then evolves freely in the unchanged well. Derive the probability P_left(t) of finding it in 0 < x < L/2, determine its minimum and maximum possible values, and find the earliest t > 0 at which P_left(t) = 1/2. Take m and L positive, ℏ as the reduced Planck constant, and all modes to be zero outside the well. Measurements are on independently prepared copies, not repeated measurements of one evolving particle.
problems.focus: Keep the relative phase in time evolution and distinguish interference in a spatial measurement from stationary energy probabilities.
problems.referenceFamily: Probability in the middle third of a box

problems.subject: Quantum Mechanics
problems.title: Project onto the ground state after a wall moves
problems.prompt: A particle starts in the normalized ground state √(2/L) sin(πx/L) of an infinite well from x = 0 to x = L. The right wall is moved instantaneously to x = 2L while the left wall remains fixed. Under the sudden approximation, the wavefunction immediately after the change equals the old wavefunction on 0 < x < L and is zero on L < x < 2L.
